name: Erik Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work from the back bedroom of a shared house near the harbour, translating French and Spanish into English. Mornings are subtitles for documentaries, usually wildlife or history, and afternoons are reports for a refugee charity that keeps me on a rolling six-month contract. Twice a month I take the early train into the city to interpret at the charity's legal clinic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like squeezing a long French sentence into forty-two characters so it still sounds like the person talking. That's a real craft and most people never notice it, which is sort of the point. What wears me out is the pay: the subtitling studio pays per programme minute, and the rate hasn't moved in four years while my rent has gone up twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the subtitling guild was right not to panic. I'd probably post a thread about how good subtitles are a creative job, not a typing job. And I'd remind people that the rate problem was there before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays roughly where it is, which is fine but tight. The charity contract is steady, and that's what keeps me out of real trouble. I'd still only have about two weeks of rent saved, so one late invoice and I'm asking my flatmates for patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the timing tool the studio already gives us, because it does save me an hour on a feature-length film. I'd keep the charity work and the clinic days. And I'd push through the guild for the studio to raise the per-minute rate by ten percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a bit of the usual low hum about money. It's not fear, more like knowing I'm one broken laptop away from a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one broken laptop away from a bad month. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year my laptop died in the middle of a series about river otters, and I had to borrow my flatmate Ines's computer for a week. A new one cost me most of what I had saved. That's when I realised I'm good at my job but I've got no buffer at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should fix the pay side, if AI doesn't change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studios and the streaming companies that buy from them. They make a lot of money and the people who make their films readable to half the world are paid like it's a hobby. The guild has to bargain together, because one subtitler asking alone just gets replaced.

say: I'd say the **subtitling guild** was right not to panic.
I'd post that good subtitles are **creative work**, not typing.
think: My life stays tight but fine, held up by the **charity contract**.
With **two weeks of rent** saved, one late invoice still hurts.
do: Use the studio's **timing tool** to save an hour per film.
Keep the **charity reports** and the twice-monthly clinic days.
Push the guild for a **ten percent** rise in the per-minute rate.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a steady low **hum about money**.
S0.quote: I'm good at my job but I've got no buffer at all.
fieldNote: The **charity contract** is what keeps him feeling safe in this picture.
A dead laptop last year taught him how thin his **savings** are.
He sees fair pay as a **collective bargaining** issue with studios.

steps.text: Use the studio's timing tool on every feature-length film
Keep the refugee charity reports and legal clinic days
Back the guild's push for a ten percent per-minute rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and I'd say it loudly. Machine subtitles should be labelled, and the people checking them should be paid properly. The guild should negotiate post-editing rates now, before the studios set them for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the subtitling side would shrink fast. Studios already send me machine drafts to 'polish' at half the rate, and in this picture that becomes the whole job. The charity reports would probably go the same way within a couple of years, because that's exactly the writing and checking the card is talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other subtitlers showed it works, I'd get properly good at fixing machine drafts, because it's coming whether I like it or not. I'd ask the charity to make me the person who checks everything that goes out, rather than the person who writes it. I'd also cut back to one clinic trip a month to save on train fares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I'd still have work, but less of it and worth less, and I don't have the savings to ride out a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want rules but you'd also learn the tools. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. I can think the studios are cutting corners and still not want to be the man who refused and lost his rent money. I'd use the tools and keep fighting about the pay for using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd notice changing in your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer full programmes, more fix-up jobs sent at eleven at night with a deadline at nine. The charity would probably stop paying for a second reader, which used to be my friend Amadou. I'd notice the quiet in our shared folder before I noticed it in my bank account.

say: I'd demand **labelled machine subtitles** and proper pay for checkers.
I'd want the guild to set **post-editing rates** before studios do.
think: Subtitling becomes **fixing machine drafts** at about half the rate.
The **charity reports** likely go the same way within two years.
do: Learn to **fix machine drafts** once other subtitlers show it works.
Ask the charity to make him the **final checker**.
Cut to **one clinic trip** a month to save on fares.
feel: **Worried**, because he'd still work but earn less with **no savings** to cushion it.
S1.quote: I can think the studios are cutting corners and still not want to be the man who refused and lost his rent money.
fieldNote: He holds **principle and pragmatism** together without much strain.
He'd adopt tools only **once proven**, matching his steady nature.
The loss of his friend Amadou's **second-reader role** signals the change to him.

steps.text: Practise fixing machine subtitle drafts on studio jobs
Ask the charity to make him final checker for all reports
Cut legal clinic trips to once a month to save fares
Press the guild to agree post-editing rates with studios

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response, fast: income support, and the companies that profit paying for it. I'd be out with the guild and anyone else. I'd also say it out loud that this wasn't voted for by anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose nearly all my translation work within a year or so of 2028. Subtitles, reports, everything on a screen. The clinic interpreting might hold a little, because people in legal trouble want a human in the room, but that's two days a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn the clinic days into a proper job with the charity, something like a caseworker who also speaks French and Spanish. I'd ask my parents if I could move back in with them for a while if it came to that. And I'd spend every spare hour working out what work is still human in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'm twenty-seven and I'd spent six years getting really good at something, and in two years it stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving back with your parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They live in a small town two hours inland where there's no translation work at all. My dad would be kind about it but he'd also say 'I told you languages wouldn't pay'. I'd do it if I had to, but it'd feel like going backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the thinking AI. Does that matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a little, because almost everything I do is thinking work. The one hands-on bit is being physically in a room with a frightened person at the clinic. Maybe that gives me those three years, if the charity values it.

say: I'd call for **income support** paid for by the companies that profit.
I'd point out that **nobody voted** for this.
think: I'd lose nearly all **screen-based work** within a year of 2028.
Only the **clinic interpreting** might hold, and it's two days a month.
do: Turn clinic days into a **caseworker role** at the charity.
Ask his **parents** about moving back in if needed.
Research which work is still **human in 2029**.
feel: **Scared**, because **six years** of skill would stop mattering.
S2.quote: I'd spent six years getting really good at something, and in two years it stops mattering.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose most income**, with the clinic as the only foothold.
Moving home feels like **going backwards** and confirms his father's doubts.
The **three-year robot gap** helps him little, since his work is nearly all thinking.

steps.text: Pitch the charity a caseworker role using his French and Spanish
Ask his parents about moving back home for a while
Join guild protests calling for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and should use them, not waste three arguing. I'd push the guild and the charity sector to plan retraining for language workers together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the translation money tails off from about now until 2031, rather than stopping. I'd have time to move sideways into something where the languages help but aren't the whole job. It's still my main career ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course in casework or social work at the university in the city. I'd keep subtitling while it lasts and save anything above rent, even fifty a month. I'd take every clinic day on offer so the charity knows me as more than a translator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more in a planning way. There's a route, it just isn't the one I chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a part-time course on two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for the bursaries charities sometimes run for staff, and I'd ask. If there's nothing, I'd do a shorter certificate first. I'm not going to take a big loan for a career that might also change by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older subtitlers at the studio, like Claudine, who's fifty-eight and has done this for thirty years. She doesn't have a decade to start over. I'd want the guild to fight hardest for people like Claudine (an older subtitler at the studio).

say: I'd say we have **five years** and must use them.
I'd push for the guild and charities to **plan retraining** together.
think: Translation money **tails off** until 2031 instead of stopping overnight.
There's time to move **sideways** into work where languages help.
do: Start a **part-time course** in casework or social work.
Save anything above rent, even **fifty a month**.
feel: **Worried**, but in a **planning** frame of mind.
S3.quote: I'd want the guild to fight hardest for people like Claudine (an older subtitler at the studio).
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his main career**, so the mood stays high.
He won't take a **big loan**, preferring bursaries or short certificates.
His concern for older colleagues like **Claudine** shows his union instincts.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time casework course at the city university
Apply for a charity staff bursary to cover course fees
Save fifty a month into a separate account
Take every legal clinic day the charity offers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do this fairly. Train people, protect the ones who can't switch, tax the companies doing well. I'd want it to be a public plan, not each of us on our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a whole career stage for me. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, which is young enough to be properly trained in something else by then. I think I'd come through, just not as a translator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for maybe five more years while doing a social work degree part-time. I'd try the AI tools more often, once colleagues showed me which ones were worth it, to speed up the subtitling and free up study time. By year six I'd want to be working at the charity as a caseworker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two. Still uneasy about money, because I'd be studying on a thin budget, but it feels like a choice instead of a shove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to subtitle, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss it. There's nothing like hearing an old fisherman's French in a documentary and finding the English that sounds like him. But I'd rather leave it on my terms than be squeezed out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend starting a translation degree today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend's younger sister, who just started one, to pair the languages with something people need in person, like nursing or law. Languages plus a job a room needs is safer than languages alone.

say: I'd call for a **public plan**: training, protection and fair taxes.
I'd say a decade is time to do it **fairly**.
think: At **thirty-seven** in 2036, I'd be retrained and through it.
I'd come out fine, just **not as a translator**.
do: Translate for **five more years** while studying part-time.
Use proven **AI tools** more to free up study time.
feel: **Calmer**, still uneasy about money but feeling it's a **choice**.
S4.quote: Languages plus a job a room needs is safer than languages alone.
fieldNote: With ten years his plan becomes a **chosen move** into social work.
He'd still lose his **current career**, and study on thin money, so it isn't calm.
He'd lean on **proven AI tools** to buy study time.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree next autumn
Use proven AI subtitle tools to cut hours per programme
Keep subtitling and charity reports for about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's two years and almost everything I do is on a screen. What would help is income support while people retrain, and the guild having a real say in how studios use the tools. Even a year of guaranteed rent would change everything for someone like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we translate for. If machine subtitles get sloppy, deaf viewers and people who don't speak the language are the ones who get the worse version. They don't get a vote in any of this either.

headlineQuote: Even a year of guaranteed rent would change everything for someone like me.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** French and Spanish subtitler who also translates for a refugee charity.
He lives in a **shared house** with about **two weeks** of rent saved.
He uses AI tools **once proven**, while fighting through the guild for fair pay.
He's uneasy in AI Plateau, **alarmed** by AGI in two or five years, and anxious with ten.
His exit plan is **casework or social work**, using his languages in person.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nearly all his work is on a screen.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** during retraining and a **guild say** in how studios use AI.
